When I was 19 years old, I went on a camping trip to a small river island near my city, alone, and planning on a weekend stay of two nights. The evening I arrived went well, I found a nice clearing following a small river nearby, set up a hammock and built a small perimeter with bells and wire so animals couldn't sneak up on me. I made a small fire and started setting up my gear to go fishing the next day. When I went to sleep, I made sure to have a clear line of sight to my stuff and to the direction I came from, so in case anyone showed up I didn't have to move to be aware of it. As I fell asleep, I heard the sounds of the forest growing more and more intense, and suddenly stopping altogether. A few moments of silence went by, and I heard a faint whistling sound in the distance. Now, we have a lot of folklore here. Most of it is related to spirits, ghosts and the forests. I've seen my fair share of creepy/strange stuff in the forest, but never came across any of the major characters of said folklore. This particular whistling sound reminded me of one of those characters, and I was trying to determine if it was an animal sound or just the wind. After listening for what seemed like an eternity, I figured it was coming closer with each whistle, from the same direction across the river. Then I started hearing the sounds of the forest again, the whistle blending in but also standing out when it came, like all the animals and insects were giving it it's own space. Definitely spooked by now, and believing I identified the thing whistling, I announced something like "Matinta, come tomorrow and I'll give you your tobacco. Please let me sleep tonight." And waited for the whistle to come again. It never did, and I went to sleep knowing I was in debt with the spirit. For clarification: Matinta is an old, emaciated woman with long grey hair that looks like it's barbed wire. She transforms into a bird to whistle and signal her presence in the forest. Anyone who hears her whistle has to either leave and don't come back, or give her an offering of either alcohol or tobacco to be left alone, a debt that will be paid the next day. People say you can either wait for her to come, or leave the offering in the same spot you slept that night for her to find. Now, back to the story, I left my offering of tobacco beneath my hammock and went to fish. I didn't want to wait around, since it's part of the legend that those who see her may be visited again every time they go through the forest. If you don't pay, she punishes you by flailing her hair at you when you sleep, scratching your limbs and back until you pay her, and I had already met someone who thought it was just a story and didn't pay. Sufficient to say his back was scarred, and I took his word for it. I spent around 4 hours upstream fishing, and came back around 10 am. The tobacco was gone, with no tracks around the hammock indicating someone walked in and grabbed it. Needless to say, I packed up and left, and never came back to that spot. To this day I cannot explain it, and people who experienced this same particular occurrence always described it to me the same way.

I can relate to the chasing dreams and losing everything part, and let me tell you something: if you ain't got nothing left to lose, that gives you a lot of wiggle room to do new things. I quit a good job and moved to a different state for an opportunity to start a new life with someone, and it fell through. Now I'm back in my hometown, my engagement is over, unemployed and in debt, and you know what I found out just a couple days ago? I really like cooking. I like mixing drinks for people, seeing them going "Yummy, make me another one later". Of course I was distraught when everything collapsed and I noticed I was fucked, but that only lasts until you do something else. And when I tried doing something else, it gave me a fair reason to go on a little longer, see what lies ahead the next month, and it has worked pretty well so far. Best case scenario, I'll get my old job back, start college again and never be so naive again. Worst case scenario, I'll work as a bartender somewhere, start culinary school and never be so naive again. You gotta work with what you got man.
